title: why sunset is the hour
hook: why sunset is the hour; every culture stopped at dusk
tomorrow: Ram Dass: we're all just walking each other home

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: silence. Your line: quiet is where it is. Which stretch of the day did you leave unfilled? What was it like in there? Day eleven.

Go outside at sunset and watch what happens to people. Someone on a balcony stops scrolling and just looks. Someone pulls over to take a photo of a sky they've seen a thousand times. The light goes gold, then orange, then that strange blue, and even busy people slow down for a second. In place after place, people have treated the end of the day as a doorway, and walked through it on purpose. This path lives at that hour. Today's word is the sun, and why its going down matters so much.
screen: `THE LIGHT GOES GOLD.` → `EVEN BUSY PEOPLE SLOW DOWN.` → `THE END OF THE DAY IS A DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: Start with how the Hebrew Bible counts a day. In Genesis, after each day of creation, the King James wording says: "And the evening and the morning were the first day." Evening first. Jewish tradition reads the day that way: the Sabbath and the festivals begin at sundown, with candles lit as the light goes. In Islam, one of the five daily prayers, called Maghrib, is prayed just after the sun sets, and during Ramadan, sunset is the moment the day's fast is broken, often with a date and water. In Christian monasteries, the evening prayer is called vespers, the Latin word for evening, and Anglican churches sing evensong. A Psalm sung at evening prayer asks that "the lifting up of my hands" be "as the evening sacrifice." In Hindu tradition, the twilights are called sandhya, the joinings, where night meets day and day meets night, and the prayers said at those hinges carry the same name. Each home has its own prayer and its own reason for it. Why sunset? Part of it is the body. Falling light is one of the signals your body uses to start winding toward sleep. Part of it is work: without lamps, when the light went, so did the working day. And part of it is simply that sunset is a bell nobody has to ring. It comes every day, for free. A doorway that opens by itself. The traditions just asked people to walk through it.
screen: `EVENING FIRST, THEN MORNING.` · `MAGHRIB, AND THE FAST BROKEN.` · `VESPERS AND THE JOININGS.` · `A BELL NOBODY HAS TO RING.` · then, large: `A DOORWAY THAT OPENS BY ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Wherever you are, find the light. A window, a lamp, the glow of the screen if that's all there is. Look at it for a breath. Then close your eyes and sit for about forty-five seconds, and let the day behind you be finished. Whatever didn't get done can wait for tomorrow's light. You're in the doorway now. The bell holds the time.
The sun. And its going down: a doorway that Jews, Muslims, Christians and Hindus each walk through in their own way. Eleventh word.
Your line: stop when the light does. Tonight, catch the moment the light changes, and stop for one breath. Just one. Let it close the day. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RAM DASS: WE'RE ALL JUST WALKING EACH OTHER HOME.`

notes: Genesis 1:5 KJV exact wording: 'And the evening and the morning were the first day.' Confirm.
Psalm 141:2 KJV: 'Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.' The script quotes two fragments; confirm.

Sandhya: some families pray at dawn, noon and dusk (three sandhyas); script says 'the twilights'. A Hindu Keeper may refine.
The index hook says 'every culture stopped at dusk'; the script avoids that universal claim and says 'in place after place'.
